title: Conference Talk Picker
statement: A one-track conference received 5,000 talk proposals, each with a fixed time slot. The organizers want to accept as many talks as possible with no two at the same time.

approaches.name: Sort by end time and keep each talk that starts after the last kept one ends
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Finishing first always leaves the most room; one sort and one pass.

approaches.name: Sort by end and use DP: best(i) = max(best(i − 1), 1 + best(last talk that ends before i starts))
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct and needed when talks have different values, but more work than the greedy rule here.

approaches.name: Keep the shortest talks first
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Wrong: a short talk across the boundary of two long talks blocks both of them.

title: Office Room Planner
statement: A company has tomorrow's 20,000 meetings with start and end times. Facilities needs the smallest number of rooms so that every meeting has a room.
constraints: Times in minutes of the day

approaches.name: Sort start times and end times separately and sweep, counting rooms in use
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: The answer is the most meetings running at once; a sweep finds it after two sorts.

approaches.name: Sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Same bound, and it can also say which room each meeting gets.

approaches.name: Count meetings at every minute of the day
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Fine for 1,440 minutes with a difference array; breaks when times are large or fractional.

approaches.name: Compare every pair of meetings for overlap
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Counting overlapping pairs does not even give the number of rooms, and is slow.

title: Shared Calendar Busy Times
statement: A team calendar shows the busy times of 8 people, 50,000 events in total, in no order. The app must show the merged busy blocks for the whole team.

approaches.name: Sort by start and merge each event into the last block when they overlap
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: After sorting, only the last block can meet the next event.

approaches.name: Sort each person's events, then merge the 8 lists with a min-heap
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Slightly faster when each person's list is already sorted.

approaches.name: Repeatedly scan all pairs and merge two overlapping events until nothing changes
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Correct but far too slow for 50,000 events.

approaches.name: Sort by end and keep events that do not overlap
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Answers a different question: it drops events instead of merging them.
